what_its_for: Ritonavir is used to treat HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) infection. It belongs to a group of medicines called protease inhibitors. It works by blocking a protein that the HIV virus needs to make copies of itself, helping to lower the amount of virus in your body. Ritonavir is almost always used in low doses alongside other HIV medicines to make those medicines work better and longer in your body.
how_to_take: Take ritonavir exactly as your doctor tells you. Always take it WITH food to help your body absorb it better and to reduce stomach upset. Swallow tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. If you are taking the oral solution (liquid), use the measuring device that came with your medicine to get the right dose. Do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take all of your HIV medicines together as part of your complete treatment plan. Never stop taking ritonavir without first talking to your doctor, even if you feel fine.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. For adults, when used to 'boost' other HIV medicines, the typical dose is 100 mg (one tablet or 1.25 mL of liquid) once or twice a day. When used as a main HIV medicine on its own, higher doses may be prescribed. For children, the dose is based on body weight and will be calculated by your doctor. Always follow the dosing schedule your doctor gives you and do not change it without asking first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is more than 4 hours before your next scheduled dose. If your next dose is coming up within 4 hours, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Missing doses can allow the virus to become harder to treat, so try to take your medicine at the same time every day. Setting a daily alarm or pill reminder may help.
storage: Tablets: Store at room temperature (below 30°C / 86°F). Keep them in the original container, away from light and moisture. Oral Solution (liquid): Store in the original bottle at room temperature. Do NOT refrigerate the liquid — cold temperatures can cause crystals to form. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all forms of ritonavir out of reach of children. Do not use the medicine if it has passed its expiration date.
what_to_avoid: Many medications can interact dangerously with ritonavir. Do NOT take ritonavir with certain medicines without your doctor's knowledge, including some heart rhythm medicines, cholesterol medicines (like simvastatin or lovastatin), certain migraine drugs, some sedatives, or some herbal products. Tell every doctor, dentist, and pharmacist you see that you take ritonavir before starting any new medicine, even ones bought without a prescription. Avoid St. John's Wort — this herbal supplement can make ritonavir much less effective. Avoid excessive alcohol while taking this medicine. Grapefruit and grapefruit juice may also affect how some medicines work alongside ritonavir, so ask your pharmacist if you are concerned.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting; yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (signs of liver problems); unusual muscle pain or weakness; fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat; signs of a serious allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing); numbness or tingling of hands or feet; changes in the way fat is distributed on your body (unusual weight gain around the belly, loss of fat from face or legs); signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst or urination; or mood changes, confusion, or difficulty thinking. Also call your doctor if you develop a new rash or if your current HIV medicines seem to stop working.
when_it_works: Ritonavir starts working in your body right away, but you will not feel a sudden change. After a few weeks, blood tests should show that the amount of HIV virus in your blood (your 'viral load') is going down and your immune system (measured by your 'CD4 count') is getting stronger. Most people do not feel sick from HIV day-to-day, so it is important to keep taking your medicine every day even when you feel well. Ritonavir controls HIV but does not cure it — stopping treatment can allow the virus to multiply again.
special_populations: Pregnancy: If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor. Ritonavir can be used during pregnancy, and treating HIV during pregnancy helps protect your baby. Breastfeeding: Women with HIV should NOT breastfeed because HIV can be passed to the baby through breast milk. Children: Ritonavir can be used in children — doses are adjusted based on body weight. The oral liquid form may be easier for young children. Older adults: Use with extra care; older patients may be more sensitive to side effects. Liver disease: If you have liver problems (including hepatitis B or C), your doctor will monitor you closely, as ritonavir can affect the liver. Kidney disease: Generally no dose adjustment is needed, but always tell your doctor about all your health conditions.
